Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Transaction Isolation Levels
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Transaction Isolation Levels

Control what each transaction can see, avoid invalid reads, and choose an isolation level that fits your workload.

Orientation

This chapter explains READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL. It shows read phenomena, practical session examples, and the trade-offs between throughput and strict correctness. Expect session commands and sample transactions to try in a safe environment.

Why this matters

Choosing the right isolation level prevents incorrect aggregates, stale reports, or unexpected transaction rollbacks in production systems.

Visual concept
MVCC snapshots & visibility
A concise visual shows transactions taking snapshots of committed rows. Snapshots control which committed rows are visible, which is why dirty reads are impossible in PostgreSQL. We’ll use this idea repeatedly when discussing each isolation level.
Explore Key Topics
Read Phenomena
Dirty, non-repeatable, phantom reads explained with examples.
Isolation Levels
Behavior of READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL.
Practical Choices
How to pick a level and handle serialization errors.
Quick facts
  • PostgreSQL supports three isolation levels; dirty reads are prevented by MVCC.
  • READ COMMITTED is default and maximizes concurrency.
  • SERIALIZABLE offers strict correctness via SSI but can produce rollbacks.
Hands-on preview

You will run two concurrent sessions to demonstrate non-repeatable reads under READ COMMITTED, and repeatable reads and serializable behaviors under stronger levels.

Takeaway

Understanding snapshots and visibility is the key to predicting and preventing surprising read behaviors in concurrent systems.

screens.title: What isolation levels control
screens.narratorSegment: Isolation levels specify how and when changes committed by one transaction become visible to other concurrent transactions. In PostgreSQL, visibility is governed by multi-version concurrency control, or MVCC, which gives each transaction a snapshot of the database at a specific point in time. That snapshot determines which committed rows you can read. Practically, this means a transaction never sees uncommitted work from another transaction, so dirty reads cannot occur. Understanding snapshots is important: if your transaction uses a snapshot taken at the start of the transaction, subsequent statements will see a consistent view according to that snapshot. If the level allows statement-level snapshots instead, each statement may observe newer committed work. The concrete effect is this: with statement-level visibility you can see updates committed between two separate select statements; with transaction-level snapshots you will not. A common misconception is thinking that isolation levels change whether writes are visible immediately to other transactions—writes are only visible when committed; isolation levels control whether newly committed writes are visible to you during your transaction. The key takeaway: isolation defines visibility windows via snapshots, and those windows are what prevent dirty reads and shape higher-level phenomena.

keyIdea.title: Snapshot-based visibility
keyIdea.text: MVCC gives each transaction a snapshot; isolation levels determine whether snapshots are per-statement or per-transaction and thereby what committed changes are visible.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › What isolation levels control
Core Concept

Snapshots and visibility

PostgreSQL’s MVCC hands each transaction a view of committed data. Isolation levels decide whether that view is fixed per-statement or per-transaction.

Why snapshots matter
  • They prevent dirty reads by exposing only committed rows.
  • They determine if subsequent statements see newly committed changes.
  • They are the foundation for preventing higher-level read phenomena.
Concrete example

If a transaction takes a transaction-level snapshot, two SELECTs in that transaction will see the same row versions even if another session commits updates between them.

Common misconception

Isolation levels do not cause uncommitted reads; PostgreSQL never exposes uncommitted changes. They control when you see newly committed changes.

Key Takeaway

Visibility is snapshot-based; isolation levels choose the snapshot boundaries that determine what committed data you can read during a transaction.

screens.title: Read phenomena: dirty, non-repeatable, phantom
screens.narratorSegment: Read phenomena are concrete ways concurrent activity can create surprising or incorrect reads. First, a dirty read happens when a transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed; if that writer later rolls back, the reader observed data that never existed. PostgreSQL’s MVCC prevents dirty reads entirely, so you won’t see uncommitted work. Second, a non-repeatable read occurs when you read the same row twice in a transaction and get different values because another transaction committed a change in between. This can happen under READ COMMITTED because each statement can see newly committed changes. Third, a phantom read happens when a repeated query that returns a set of rows returns a different set on re-execution because new rows were inserted or deleted by a concurrent committed transaction. Phantoms affect queries over ranges or predicates rather than a single row. A useful test: start a transaction, run a SELECT that counts rows matching a condition, have another session insert a matching row and commit, then re-run the SELECT. If you see an additional row, you observed a phantom. Misconception to avoid: phantoms are not merely changed values on existing rows—they are about the set of rows returned by a query changing. Understanding these distinctions helps you map behaviors to the proper isolation level.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Read phenomena
Definition

Dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads

These phenomena describe how repeated reads can return unexpected data when other transactions commit concurrent changes.

Dirty read

Reading uncommitted data. PostgreSQL’s MVCC prevents this; you only see committed rows.

Non-repeatable read

You read a row, another transaction commits an update, and your second read sees a different value. This is allowed in READ COMMITTED.

Phantom read

A repeated query returns a changed set of rows because another committed transaction inserted or deleted matching rows.

Quick test

Run a COUNT in one session, insert a matching row in another and commit, then re-run the COUNT to detect a phantom.

Key Takeaway

Different phenomena require different isolation guarantees; knowing the exact phenomenon helps pick the right isolation level.

screens.title: READ COMMITTED (default)
screens.narratorSegment: READ COMMITTED is PostgreSQL’s default isolation level and it provides statement-level visibility: each statement sees data committed before that statement began. The immediate consequence is that dirty reads are impossible, yet you can observe non-repeatable reads or phantoms when another transaction commits between two statements. A concrete example is an aggregate: start a transaction and run a SUM, then a concurrent session updates the underlying rows and commits; if you re-run the SUM in your transaction you will observe the updated total because each statement reevaluates visibility relative to when the statement begins. This behavior is often desirable for interactive applications: it allows high concurrency and ensures that each statement reads the most recently committed data available at that moment. A common misconception is that using READ COMMITTED within a multi-statement transaction guarantees the same view across statements — it does not. If you need identical row versions across statements, you should use a stronger level. When designing queries, remember READ COMMITTED favors throughput and simplicity, but you must accept that repeated reads within one transaction can return different results. For many web workloads where each request is short and sees the latest committed state, READ COMMITTED is the pragmatic default.

For many web workloads where each request is short and sees the latest committed state, READ COMMITTED is the pragmatic default.

keyIdea.title: READ COMMITTED
keyIdea.text: Default mode: prevents dirty reads, provides statement-level visibility, and can show non-repeatable and phantom reads between statements.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › READ COMMITTED
Comparison

READ COMMITTED behavior

Each statement sees data committed before the statement begins. This avoids dirty reads but allows later statements to observe newly committed changes.

When to use

Interactive web requests and operations where seeing the latest committed data per statement is preferred over strict repeatability.

Misconception

Repeated reads in a transaction are not guaranteed to be the same; each statement may see newly committed changes.

Concrete session example
-- Session 1
BEGIN;
SELECT SUM(sale_amount) FROM sales_data WHERE product_name = 'Widget A';
-- Session 2 updates and commits
-- Session 1 re-runs:
SELECT SUM(sale_amount) FROM sales_data WHERE product_name = 'Widget A';
COMMIT;
Key Takeaway

READ COMMITTED maximizes concurrency by letting each statement see the most recent committed state at its start; it does not provide repeatable reads across statements.

screens.title: REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL
screens.narratorSegment: REPEATABLE READ gives a transaction a consistent snapshot taken at the beginning of the transaction, ensuring that any row read once will return the same version for the lifetime of that transaction. In the S Q L standard, REPEATABLE READ does not necessarily prevent phantom reads, but PostgreSQL’s implementation is stronger: it uses a snapshot at transaction start and prevents phantoms by ensuring queries see a consistent set of rows from that snapshot. The practical result is that repeated SELECTs and aggregate queries will return identical results even if other transactions commit inserts or updates afterward. However, this stronger guarantee introduces a behavioral nuance: if your transaction attempts to update or delete a row that was changed by another transaction committed after your snapshot was taken, PostgreSQL will detect the write conflict and raise a serialization error, causing your transaction to roll back. That rollback is a safety mechanism to preserve repeatability. A common misunderstanding is thinking REPEATABLE READ eliminates all conflicts; it prevents read anomalies but transfers some conflict handling into write-time rollbacks. When you need consistent reads across multiple statements and are prepared to retry failed updates, REPEATABLE READ is an appropriate choice.

keyIdea.title: REPEATABLE READ
keyIdea.text: A transaction sees a single snapshot from its start; PostgreSQL’s implementation yields repeatable reads and prevents phantoms but may raise serialization errors on conflicting writes.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › REPEATABLE READ
Process

Transaction-level snapshot

A single snapshot at transaction start guarantees that repeated reads return the same row versions, and PostgreSQL extends this to prevent phantoms.

Behavioral note

Writes that conflict with rows changed after your snapshot may cause a serialization error when you try to commit.

When to use

When you need consistent reads across multiple statements and can handle occasional retries on write conflicts.

Concrete example

Begin a REPEATABLE READ transaction, run aggregates and counts; even if another session commits inserts, your queries will see the original snapshot. If you attempt to update a row that was updated by the concurrent commit, PostgreSQL will raise a serialization error at commit time.

Key Takeaway

REPEATABLE READ provides consistent snapshots that prevent non-repeatable and, in PostgreSQL, phantom reads, at the cost of possible serialization rollbacks on conflicting updates.

screens.title: SERIALIZABLE and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)
screens.narratorSegment: SERIALIZABLE is the strictest isolation level. Its guarantee is that concurrent transactions will produce results equivalent to some serial execution order. PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation, or SSI, which tracks dependencies and detects cycles that would create anomalies. When SSI detects that completing a transaction would violate serializability, it aborts and raises a serialization error, forcing the application to retry the transaction if it needs to complete. Practically, SERIALIZABLE prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads, producing audit-quality consistency. The trade-off is that higher contention increases the likelihood of serialization errors and requires retry logic in the application. A common misconception is assuming SERIALIZABLE simply locks more aggressively; instead, PostgreSQL uses dependency tracking and targeted aborts rather than global serial execution. Use SERIALIZABLE when correctness must mirror a serial schedule, as in financial reconciliations, and when your system can tolerate occasional retries. Understanding SSI’s detection model helps you predict when retries will be necessary and design transactions to minimize conflicts. SERIALIZABLE and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) means serializable ensures results equivalent to serial execution using ssi; conflicts lead to serialization errors and transaction retries to preserve correctness.. In practical terms, strongest guarantee and how postgresql enforces serializability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › SERIALIZABLE
Architecture

Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)

PostgreSQL enforces serializability by tracking dependencies between transactions and aborting those that would create non-serializable outcomes.

How SSI works

It observes read-write dependencies and detects cycles; when a problematic cycle is detected, one transaction is rolled back to maintain a serial order.

When to prefer SERIALIZABLE

Use it for audit-level reports or financial tasks that require a view consistent with some serial execution.

Practical trade-off

Stronger guarantees increase the chance of serialization errors and require retry logic, which can reduce throughput under contention.

Key Takeaway

SERIALIZABLE preserves serial equivalence using SSI; prepare for retries when conflicts are likely.

screens.title: READ UNCOMMITTED vs PostgreSQL behavior
screens.narratorSegment: The S Q L standard defines a READ UNCOMMITTED level that would allow dirty reads. PostgreSQL does not implement READ UNCOMMITTED in practice; if you request it, PostgreSQL behaves like READ COMMITTED. This behavior stems from PostgreSQL’s MVCC model, which never exposes uncommitted row versions to other transactions. The practical implication is simple: you cannot force PostgreSQL to perform dirty reads because its storage and visibility rules prevent it. A misconception to avoid is assuming READ UNCOMMITTED will give you higher performance at the cost of correctness in PostgreSQL; it will not change read visibility. Instead, if you need lower overhead than READ COMMITTED and are exploring unconventional patterns, recall that PostgreSQL’s MVCC already provides efficient concurrent access without exposing uncommitted work. When documenting or configuring systems, write that PostgreSQL supports READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE, and treat READ UNCOMMITTED as an alias for READ COMMITTED in this environment. This clarity prevents configuration mistakes and sets correct expectations about what visibility options the server actually provides. In practical terms, why read uncommitted behaves like read committed in postgresql. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › READ UNCOMMITTED
Comparison

READ UNCOMMITTED behavior in PostgreSQL

Although the standard lists a READ UNCOMMITTED level that allows dirty reads, PostgreSQL’s MVCC never exposes uncommitted data, so the mode behaves like READ COMMITTED.

Why

MVCC stores multiple versions and only shows committed versions; uncommitted rows are not visible to other transactions.

Practical note

When configuring, treat READ UNCOMMITTED as an alias for READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL and avoid relying on dirty-read semantics.

Key Takeaway

PostgreSQL’s MVCC prevents dirty reads, so READ UNCOMMITTED offers no weaker visibility than READ COMMITTED in this system.

screens.title: Setting isolation levels with SQL
screens.narratorSegment: You can control isolation in PostgreSQL for a single transaction or for the whole session. For a single transaction, run SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL followed by the desired level after BEGIN. For session-wide changes that affect subsequent transactions, use SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL. Practically, prefer setting the level per transaction when only a single operation needs stronger guarantees; use session-level settings when all activity on a connection needs the same behavior. Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Setting isolation levels
Code Walkthrough

Session and transaction examples

-- Per-transaction
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- do reads and writes
COMMIT;

-- Per-session
SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
BEGIN;
-- subsequent transactions start with REPEATABLE READ
COMMIT;

Remember: SET TRANSACTION must be executed after BEGIN for the current transaction. SET SESSION affects transactions started later on the connection.

Practical tip

Prefer per-transaction settings when only a critical operation needs higher guarantees; this minimizes the impact on concurrency and reduces the surface for serialization errors.

Key Takeaway

Choose scope carefully: per-transaction for targeted consistency, per-session for broad defaults. Pair SERIALIZABLE with retry logic.

screens.title: Choosing an isolation level
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right isolation level depends on your application's consistency needs and tolerance for retries. Start by asking whether each transaction must reflect a single, consistent database state. If yes, SERIALIZABLE is the right fit because it guarantees serial equivalence, though you must accept the potential for serialization errors and add retry logic. If you need consistent reads across multiple statements but prefer fewer rollbacks, REPEATABLE READ often fits: it gives a transaction a single snapshot and prevents non-repeatable and, in PostgreSQL, phantom reads, while still creating conflicts that can cause rollbacks on writes. For interactive applications where users expect to see the latest committed data and throughput is critical, READ COMMITTED provides the best concurrency: it avoids dirty reads and shows the most recent committed data at each statement, but repeated reads within a transaction can differ. A common design pattern is to limit the use of the strongest level to short, critical transactions, and to structure transactions to minimize overlapping writes. Misconception: stronger isolation is always better; in reality, overusing SERIALIZABLE can increase application complexity and reduce throughput without providing practical benefits for many workloads. Choose thoughtfully and test under realistic concurrency.

screens.title: Handling serialization errors and retries
screens.narratorSegment: Serialization errors occur when PostgreSQL detects that completing a transaction would violate serializability under SSI. These errors are a safety mechanism: PostgreSQL aborts the transaction to prevent an outcome that could not happen in any serial execution. When designing systems, expect and handle these errors explicitly: catch the serialization error in your application, back off if appropriate, and retry the transaction. Keep retries short and idempotent when possible. Structuring transactions to touch fewer rows and to perform reads before writes reduces the window for conflicts and lowers retry frequency. A common mistake is to retry long-running transactions without adding a delay or reducing their footprint; this increases contention and the likelihood of repeated failures. Another strategy is to move non-critical work outside the critical transaction so that the protected transaction remains compact. Remember that retries under SERIALIZABLE are a feature, not a bug—they ensure correctness by enforcing serial equivalence. The key operational takeaway: add retry logic, make transactions compact and idempotent where possible, and measure retry rates under realistic concurrency before choosing SERIALIZABLE in production. Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Handling serialization errors
Process

Retry strategy and conflict reduction

Why rollback happens

SSI detects dependency cycles that would break serial equivalence and aborts one transaction to avoid an invalid result.

Retry pattern
  1. Catch the serialization error in application code.
  2. Back off briefly if contention is high.
  3. Retry the transaction with the same logic.
Conflict reduction

Keep transactions short, touch fewer rows, perform reads before writes, and move non-critical work outside the critical section.

Key Takeaway

Treat serialization errors as expected behavior under SERIALIZABLE; design transactions to minimize them and implement robust retry logic.

screens.title: Hands-on walkthrough: reporting example
screens.narratorSegment: Use the provided sales_data table to observe behaviors under different isolation levels. Begin by creating the table and inserting two rows, then open two psql sessions. To demonstrate a non-repeatable read under READ COMMITTED, start a transaction in session one, run an aggregate on Widget A, and do not commit. In session two, update the sale_amount for Widget A and commit. Back in session one, re-run the aggregate and observe the changed sum. This shows READ COMMITTED allows statement-level visibility. Next, try REPEATABLE READ by starting a transaction with that isolation level in session one and repeating the same sequence: the second SELECT in session one returns the original sum because the transaction’s snapshot predates session two’s commit. Also test phantom behavior by counting rows matching a pattern, then inserting a new matching row in the concurrent session and committing. Under REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL, your count will not include the new row; the snapshot prevents phantoms. If you attempt to update the same row in REPEATABLE READ after concurrent modification, expect a serialization error at commit. These experiments make the abstract definitions concrete and let you observe the trade-offs firsthand.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a practical understanding of transaction isolation levels and how PostgreSQL uses them to manage concurrent data access. You'll learn the three isolation levels PostgreSQL supports, why dirty reads never occur under its multi-version concurrency control, and how different levels allow or prevent non-repeatable reads and phantom reads. We'll step through concrete session examples so you can see the visible effects when two sessions interact, and we'll discuss the trade-offs: higher consistency means more risk of transaction rollbacks and lower concurrency. By the end you should be able to choose the isolation level that fits reporting, interactive web updates, or financial auditing situations, and know when to expect serialization errors and how to handle them. This orientation sets the frame: isolation controls visibility, MVCC enforces no dirty reads, and PostgreSQL’s REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE provide stronger guarantees at a concurrency cost. Keep in mind the practical question you’ll return to: do you need the absolute serializability of SERIALIZABLE, or will READ COMMITTED’s concurrency be enough for your application?

Over the next screens you'll acquire four practical skills. First, you will explain why isolation levels exist and how they shape visibility between concurrent transactions; that helps you reason about bugs that only appear under load. Second, you will describe the standard isolation levels and the three read phenomena they aim to control: dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads; having these definitions prevents confusion when comparing behaviors. Third, you will detail PostgreSQL’s implementations of READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE, including PostgreSQL’s snapshot semantics and how REPEATABLE READ prevents phantoms in practice; this knowledge lets you pick the right mode for reports or interactive updates. Fourth, you will choose an isolation level for specific application needs, weighing consistency against concurrency and planning for serialization retries when necessary. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue so you can recall when to use each level. By the end you should be able to justify an isolation choice for a reporting job, a web request, or an audit process.

On this secondary objectives screen we'll focus on applied outcomes. You will run paired sessions to observe non-repeatable reads under READ COMMITTED and to confirm snapshot isolation under REPEATABLE READ. You will learn how to interpret a serialization error: why it happens, what it means for consistency, and when to retry. You will also gain the judgment to recommend READ COMMITTED for responsive web interactions where seeing the latest committed data matters, or SERIALIZABLE for audit-quality reports where perfect consistency is required. Each objective connects to a hands-on task so you practice seeing and resolving the behaviors described. As you use session commands and the small schema provided, pay attention to how PostgreSQL's MVCC ensures committed visibility and how Serializability uses detection to preserve the illusion of serial execution. These applied abilities let you both verify system behavior and make informed design decisions.

Isolation levels specify how and when changes committed by one transaction become visible to other concurrent transactions. In PostgreSQL, visibility is governed by multi-version concurrency control, or MVCC, which gives each transaction a snapshot of the database at a specific point in time. That snapshot determines which committed rows you can read. Practically, this means a transaction never sees uncommitted work from another transaction, so dirty reads cannot occur. Understanding snapshots is important: if your transaction uses a snapshot taken at the start of the transaction, subsequent statements will see a consistent view according to that snapshot. If the level allows statement-level snapshots instead, each statement may observe newer committed work. The concrete effect is this: with statement-level visibility you can see updates committed between two separate select statements; with transaction-level snapshots you will not. A common misconception is thinking that isolation levels change whether writes are visible immediately to other transactions—writes are only visible when committed; isolation levels control whether newly committed writes are visible to you during your transaction. The key takeaway: isolation defines visibility windows via snapshots, and those windows are what prevent dirty reads and shape higher-level phenomena.

Read phenomena are concrete ways concurrent activity can create surprising or incorrect reads. First, a dirty read happens when a transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed; if that writer later rolls back, the reader observed data that never existed. PostgreSQL’s MVCC prevents dirty reads entirely, so you won’t see uncommitted work. Second, a non-repeatable read occurs when you read the same row twice in a transaction and get different values because another transaction committed a change in between. This can happen under READ COMMITTED because each statement can see newly committed changes. Third, a phantom read happens when a repeated query that returns a set of rows returns a different set on re-execution because new rows were inserted or deleted by a concurrent committed transaction. Phantoms affect queries over ranges or predicates rather than a single row. A useful test: start a transaction, run a SELECT that counts rows matching a condition, have another session insert a matching row and commit, then re-run the SELECT. If you see an additional row, you observed a phantom. Misconception to avoid: phantoms are not merely changed values on existing rows—they are about the set of rows returned by a query changing. Understanding these distinctions helps you map behaviors to the proper isolation level.

READ COMMITTED is PostgreSQL’s default isolation level and it provides statement-level visibility: each statement sees data committed before that statement began. The immediate consequence is that dirty reads are impossible, yet you can observe non-repeatable reads or phantoms when another transaction commits between two statements. A concrete example is an aggregate: start a transaction and run a SUM, then a concurrent session updates the underlying rows and commits; if you re-run the SUM in your transaction you will observe the updated total because each statement reevaluates visibility relative to when the statement begins. This behavior is often desirable for interactive applications: it allows high concurrency and ensures that each statement reads the most recently committed data available at that moment. A common misconception is that using READ COMMITTED within a multi-statement transaction guarantees the same view across statements — it does not. If you need identical row versions across statements, you should use a stronger level. When designing queries, remember READ COMMITTED favors throughput and simplicity, but you must accept that repeated reads within one transaction can return different results. For many web workloads where each request is short and sees the latest committed state, READ COMMITTED is the pragmatic default.

REPEATABLE READ gives a transaction a consistent snapshot taken at the beginning of the transaction, ensuring that any row read once will return the same version for the lifetime of that transaction. In the S Q L standard, REPEATABLE READ does not necessarily prevent phantom reads, but PostgreSQL’s implementation is stronger: it uses a snapshot at transaction start and prevents phantoms by ensuring queries see a consistent set of rows from that snapshot. The practical result is that repeated SELECTs and aggregate queries will return identical results even if other transactions commit inserts or updates afterward. However, this stronger guarantee introduces a behavioral nuance: if your transaction attempts to update or delete a row that was changed by another transaction committed after your snapshot was taken, PostgreSQL will detect the write conflict and raise a serialization error, causing your transaction to roll back. That rollback is a safety mechanism to preserve repeatability. A common misunderstanding is thinking REPEATABLE READ eliminates all conflicts; it prevents read anomalies but transfers some conflict handling into write-time rollbacks. When you need consistent reads across multiple statements and are prepared to retry failed updates, REPEATABLE READ is an appropriate choice.

SERIALIZABLE is the strictest isolation level. Its guarantee is that concurrent transactions will produce results equivalent to some serial execution order. PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation, or SSI, which tracks dependencies and detects cycles that would create anomalies. When SSI detects that completing a transaction would violate serializability, it aborts and raises a serialization error, forcing the application to retry the transaction if it needs to complete. Practically, SERIALIZABLE prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads, producing audit-quality consistency. The trade-off is that higher contention increases the likelihood of serialization errors and requires retry logic in the application. A common misconception is assuming SERIALIZABLE simply locks more aggressively; instead, PostgreSQL uses dependency tracking and targeted aborts rather than global serial execution. Use SERIALIZABLE when correctness must mirror a serial schedule, as in financial reconciliations, and when your system can tolerate occasional retries. Understanding SSI’s detection model helps you predict when retries will be necessary and design transactions to minimize conflicts. In practical terms, strongest guarantee and how postgresql enforces serializability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The S Q L standard defines a READ UNCOMMITTED level that would allow dirty reads. PostgreSQL does not implement READ UNCOMMITTED in practice; if you request it, PostgreSQL behaves like READ COMMITTED. This behavior stems from PostgreSQL’s MVCC model, which never exposes uncommitted row versions to other transactions. The practical implication is simple: you cannot force PostgreSQL to perform dirty reads because its storage and visibility rules prevent it. A misconception to avoid is assuming READ UNCOMMITTED will give you higher performance at the cost of correctness in PostgreSQL; it will not change read visibility. Instead, if you need lower overhead than READ COMMITTED and are exploring unconventional patterns, recall that PostgreSQL’s MVCC already provides efficient concurrent access without exposing uncommitted work. When documenting or configuring systems, write that PostgreSQL supports READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE, and treat READ UNCOMMITTED as an alias for READ COMMITTED in this environment. This clarity prevents configuration mistakes and sets correct expectations about what visibility options the server actually provides. Choosing the right isolation level depends on your application's consistency needs and tolerance for retries. Start by asking whether each transaction must reflect a single, consistent database state. If yes, SERIALIZABLE is the right fit because it guarantees serial equivalence, though you must accept the potential for serialization errors and add retry logic. If you need consistent reads across multiple statements but prefer fewer rollbacks, REPEATABLE READ often fits: it gives a transaction a single snapshot and prevents non-repeatable and, in PostgreSQL, phantom reads, while still creating conflicts that can cause rollbacks on writes. For interactive applications where users expect to see the latest committed data and throughput is critical, READ COMMITTED provides the best concurrency: it avoids dirty reads and shows the most recent committed data at each statement, but repeated reads within a transaction can differ. A common design pattern is to limit the use of the strongest level to short, critical transactions, and to structure transactions to minimize overlapping writes. Misconception: stronger isolation is always better; in reality, overusing SERIALIZABLE can increase application complexity and reduce throughput without providing practical benefits for many workloads. Choose thoughtfully and test under realistic concurrency.

Serialization errors occur when PostgreSQL detects that completing a transaction would violate serializability under SSI. These errors are a safety mechanism: PostgreSQL aborts the transaction to prevent an outcome that could not happen in any serial execution. When designing systems, expect and handle these errors explicitly: catch the serialization error in your application, back off if appropriate, and retry the transaction. Keep retries short and idempotent when possible. Structuring transactions to touch fewer rows and to perform reads before writes reduces the window for conflicts and lowers retry frequency. A common mistake is to retry long-running transactions without adding a delay or reducing their footprint; this increases contention and the likelihood of repeated failures. Another strategy is to move non-critical work outside the critical transaction so that the protected transaction remains compact. Remember that retries under SERIALIZABLE are a feature, not a bug—they ensure correctness by enforcing serial equivalence. The key operational takeaway: add retry logic, make transactions compact and idempotent where possible, and measure retry rates under realistic concurrency before choosing SERIALIZABLE in production. To finish, hold three compact ideas in mind. First, PostgreSQL’s MVCC prevents dirty reads: you will never read uncommitted data. Second, READ COMMITTED provides statement-level visibility and is the default for interactive workloads, but it allows non-repeatable and phantom reads within a transaction. Third, both REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE strengthen consistency: REPEATABLE READ gives a transaction a start-time snapshot and prevents phantoms in PostgreSQL, while SERIALIZABLE guarantees results equivalent to some serial execution via Serializable Snapshot Isolation and can trigger serialization errors that require retries. When choosing an isolation level, balance correctness needs against application complexity and throughput; use practical experiments to validate behavior under realistic concurrency.
